stemBlocks.value: A cylindrical water container of radius 12 cm and height 20 cm is completely filled with water, and a pipe at its base dispenses the water into cone-shaped cups of radius 3 cm and height 8 cm. (a) Calculate the volume of water in the cylindrical container, in litres, correct to 2 decimal places. (1 000 cm³ = 1 litre)
Think first: Part (a) only asks about the cylinder, so the cone measurements are not needed yet.

stemBlocks.altText: Source visual for edmar-csec-p047-q11 from workbook page 47.

solutionSteps.instruction: Write down the formula for the volume of a cylinder.

contentBlocks.value: r is the radius, h is the height

solutionSteps.instruction: Substitute r = 12 cm and h = 20 cm.
Evaluate using the π key on your calculator.
Convert to litres by dividing by 1 000.

contentBlocks.value: the third decimal is 7, so round the second up

strategyBlocks.value: Use V = πr²h with r = 12 cm and h = 20 cm to get the volume in cm³, then divide by 1 000 to convert to litres.

whyThisWorks.value: A cylinder is a prism with a circular cross-section, so its volume is just the area of the circular base, πr², stacked through the height h. Because every horizontal slice is the same circle, multiplying base area by height counts the whole solid exactly once. Converting cm³ to litres is a matter of scale only: 1 000 identical cubic centimetres fill one litre, so the number of litres is always the number of cubic centimetres divided by 1 000.

commonErrors.misconception: Using the diameter 12 cm as if it were the radius, or halving the 12 cm when it is already the radius.

commonErrors.misconception: Multiplying by 1 000 instead of dividing when converting cm³ to litres.
